edges.description: Infiltrating leukocytes drive transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium-sized muscular arteries.
Sustained arterial inflammation drives systemic constitutional symptoms.
Vessel-wall necrosis, stenosis, thrombosis, and microaneurysm rupture impair downstream organ perfusion.
Transmural arterial necrosis manifests histopathologically as necrotizing vasculitis.
Inflammatory destruction of medium-sized muscular arteries produces medium-vessel vasculitis.
Medial destruction and intimal remodeling produce characteristic microaneurysms and stenoses on angiography.
Necrotizing inflammation of dermal and subcutaneous medium-to-small arteries produces cutaneous vasculitis.
Chronic systemic inflammation drives catabolic weight loss.
Systemic vascular and intramuscular inflammation causes diffuse myalgias.
Multifocal arterial ischemia produces multiorgan dysfunction and potential polyvisceral failure.
Ischemia of the vasa nervorum causes axonal mononeuropathy multiplex or polyneuropathy.
Renal interlobar and arcuate artery stenosis induces renin-mediated renovascular hypertension.
Cutaneous and subcutaneous arterial hypoperfusion produces livedo reticularis.
Testicular artery vasculitis and ischemia cause painful orchitis.
Dermal/subcutaneous medium-vessel ischemia and inflammation produce skin manifestations.
Vasa nervorum and cerebral arterial ischemia produce peripheral and central nervous system manifestations.
Mesenteric arterial stenosis, thrombosis, or hemorrhage causes gastrointestinal ischemia.

nodes.description: Luminal narrowing, thrombosis, and hemorrhage across medium-sized visceral, renal, neural (vasa nervorum), cutaneous, and testicular arteries cause downstream tissue ischemia and infarction, ranging from single-organ involvement to life-threatening mesenteric, renal, cardiac, or cerebral events and polyvisceral failure.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical Approach to Diagnosis and Therapy of Polyarteritis Nodosa.
evidence.snippet: Idiopathic and hereditary variants of polyarteritis nodosa are treated with immunomodulatory medications such as glucocorticoids, conventional immunomodulatory drugs (e.g., cyclophosphamide) and biologic agents (e.g., tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, interleukin 6 inhibitor), while hepatitis B virus-associated polyarteritis nodosa primarily requires antiviral therapy combined with plasma exchange.

nodes.description: Non-severe or remission-maintenance primary PAN is managed with conventional non-cyclophosphamide immunosuppressant medications tailored to disease severity to maintain vascular disease control while limiting cumulative glucocorticoid and alkylator toxicity.

nodes.description: In primary (idiopathic, non-HBV) PAN, an incompletely defined immune trigger recruits T lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils into the walls of medium-sized muscular arteries in the absence of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies or immune-complex glomerulonephritis; responsiveness to systemic immunosuppression supports an active immunopathogenic process.
